value.overview: The Flame-colored Tanager is a striking medium-sized songbird of mountain forests from Mexico through Central America to Panama. Adult males are bright orange-red or flame-colored, while females are yellowish or olive with strong back streaking. Both sexes show two bold white wingbars, white spots on the wing feathers and tail, and a dark ear patch. It usually lives high in trees and may occur alone, in pairs, or in mixed-species flocks.
value.classification: The Flame-colored Tanager belongs to the order Passeriformes and family Cardinalidae, the cardinal and grosbeak family. Its scientific name is Piranga bidentata.
value.identification: This tanager measures about 18–19 centimeters long. The male is orange-red to flame-orange, with a darker ear patch, streaked upperparts, dark wings, two prominent white wingbars, and white spots on the wing and tail feathers. The female is mainly yellow or olive-yellow, with similar wing markings and a streaked back. In Costa Rica, the species can be distinguished from other Piranga tanagers by its bold double wingbars and strongly streaked mantle.
value.rangeHabitat: The Flame-colored Tanager ranges from Mexico through Guatemala, Honduras, El Salvador, Nicaragua, Costa Rica, and western Panama. In Costa Rica it is a resident of the Central Volcanic Cordillera, Talamanca Cordillera, and the Dota region. It is most often found in humid montane and evergreen forest, forest edges, wooded pastures, coffee plantations, gardens, and other areas with mature trees. Costa Rican records generally span middle and high elevations, with broader occurrence on the Pacific slope and occasional descent to about 900 meters.
value.migrationStatus: Generally resident in Costa Rica, with possible local elevational movements. It occurs year-round in the Costa Rican highlands rather than arriving as a regular long-distance migrant.
value.breeding: In Costa Rica, breeding is reported mainly from April through June, although timing can vary with location and conditions. The female builds a loose open cup from twigs, rootlets, vine tendrils, grasses, and other plant fibers. The nest is usually placed in dense foliage or a tree fork about 5–11 meters above the ground, sometimes in a cypress or other tall tree. Clutches commonly contain two or three pale blue eggs marked with reddish-brown or dark lavender spots.
value.dietFeeding: The Flame-colored Tanager feeds on insects and other small arthropods, along with berries and other soft fruits. It forages mainly in the middle and upper levels of trees, gleaning prey from foliage and branches and taking fruit from shrubs and forest trees. It may eat army ants and can search vegetation methodically while moving alone or with a mate. Fruit resources are especially important outside periods of intensive breeding activity.
value.behavior: This species is usually quiet and unobtrusive despite its bright plumage. It is most often seen alone or in pairs, though it sometimes joins mixed-species feeding flocks. Individuals forage through tree crowns and forest edges, commonly remaining high above the ground. Its song consists of a short series of somewhat buzzy or burry notes separated by pauses, and its calls include clear, strong, rolled notes.
